definition: requiring great effort; difficult and tiring
memoryTip: Arduous sounds like “argh!” — hard work that makes you groan.
correctPassage: Mapping the remote canyon required an arduous trek across scree slopes and frozen streams.
wrongPassages: After the arduous lecture ended early, students left feeling refreshed and ready for the exam.
The committee chose the arduous option because it demanded almost no preparation.
Her arduous smile suggested she found the whole ordeal pleasantly effortless.

memoryTip: In + consequence → without consequences → doesn’t matter.
correctPassage: Historians dismissed the spelling change as inconsequential beside the treaty’s territorial concessions.
wrongPassages: The inconsequential discovery overturned decades of accepted theory in a single paper.
Diplomats treated the border dispute as inconsequential only after armies massed on both sides.
She hoped to inconsequential the budget shortfall by delaying every nonessential purchase.

memoryTip: In-superable: you can’t “get over” it — like an unclimbable wall.
correctPassage: Language barriers proved insuperable until a bilingual mediator joined the negotiations.
wrongPassages: The obstacle was insuperable for only a moment before the team cleared it with ease.
Critics praised his insuperable style for how flexible and open to revision it remained.
She found the puzzle insuperable once every clue had already been solved for her.

definition: an opinion formed without complete evidence; a guess
memoryTip: Con + ject (throw) → throw out a guess before the proof is in.
correctPassage: Without sealed archives, scholars could only conjecture about the author’s motives for leaving.
wrongPassages: The lab recorded the conjecture on a digital scale as exactly one gram of salt.
Once DNA results arrived, every claim became a verified fact—no conjecture remained to discuss.
She packed a spare conjecture in the trunk next to the tire and jumper cables.

definition: relating to what did not happen but might have; contrary to fact
memoryTip: Counter + fact → against what actually happened; pure “what if?”
correctPassage: The seminar traced a counterfactual path: how trade might have shifted had the canal never opened.
wrongPassages: Eyewitnesses supplied a counterfactual account that matched every timestamp on the security tape.
The census report was counterfactual in its careful listing of each household surveyed.
Engineers preferred counterfactual steel because it never warped under load.
